response:
A content delivery network, or CDN, helps web pages and videos load quickly no matter where a visitor is located. Normally, every request for a website travels to one origin server — the single original computer, often far away, that stores the real files. If millions of people request the same page at once, that long trip creates delays and overload. A CDN solves this by copying the site's files onto many computers scattered around the world, called edge locations, positioned close to where people actually live. When a request comes in, it gets routed to the nearest edge location instead of the distant original. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries stocking copies of a popular new book, so nobody has to travel across the country to the one publisher's warehouse to read it. If the nearby location already has a fresh copy of the requested file, that's called a cache hit, and the page appears almost instantly. If not, that location fetches a copy from the origin server, saves it for next time, and delivery gets faster for future visitors. This system also spreads out traffic so no single server gets overwhelmed during busy periods, and it keeps things running smoothly even if one location has trouble, since others nearby can step in.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's real files | It's the ultimate source everything else copies from |
| Edge location | A nearby computer holding copies of site files | It shortens the distance data has to travel |
| Cache hit | When a nearby copy is already available | It makes loading nearly instant |
| Latency | The delay caused by distance and traffic | Reducing it is the whole point of a CDN |
